title: Associative entities for many-to-many relationships
description: A practical guide to modeling many-to-many relationships without losing attributes that belong to the relationship itself.
lead: When two entity tables have a many-to-many relationship, the important data often lives between them. A product can appear in many campaigns, and a campaign can contain many products. The product name belongs to the product. The campaign name belongs to the campaign. But the promotional price, display placement, and quantity cap belong to the specific product-in-campaign relationship. An associative entity preserves those facts at the correct grain instead of forcing them into either side.

sections.heading: The flattening mistake
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail dataset with products and marketing campaigns. Products are stable sellable items. Campaigns are planned merchandising events. The business question is not only which products exist or which campaigns exist. Analysts also need to know which product was selected for which campaign, at what promotional price, in which placement, and with what unit cap.

A tempting shortcut is to add campaign columns to the product table. That seems convenient while each product appears in only one campaign. It breaks as soon as the same product appears in two campaigns with different relationship attributes.

In this hypothetical data, product P100 is a notebook. It appears in a Back to School campaign at 3.99 and in a Clearance campaign at 2.99. If campaign_id, campaign_name, promo_price, and placement are placed directly on product, there is no single correct value for P100. Repeating product rows then corrupts the product grain: one product becomes two rows because of campaign participation, not because there are two products.

The opposite flattening fails too. Adding product_1_id, product_2_id, product_3_id, and matching price columns to campaign preserves one row per campaign only by imposing an arbitrary maximum number of products. It also makes every product-specific attribute position-dependent. A query for all products priced below 3.00 must scan multiple column sets, and adding a fourth product changes the table design rather than adding a row.

The modeling error is not merely aesthetic. It puts facts at the wrong grain. Product_name depends on product_id. Campaign_name depends on campaign_id. Promo_price in this example depends on the pair campaign_id and product_id. The pair is the candidate key for the relationship when each product appears at most once in a campaign. Data normalization literature describes this style of reasoning in terms of dependencies: attributes should depend on the key of the relation that contains them.

sections.heading: Model the relationship as its own entity
paragraphs: An associative entity is a table whose rows represent instances of a relationship between two or more entities. For this example, the associative entity is campaign_product. Its grain is one product selected for one campaign. The table has foreign keys to campaign and product, plus attributes that describe that particular selection.

This is different from treating the table as an implementation detail called a join table. A pure join table may only contain two foreign keys. An associative entity has business meaning: it can have its own attributes, rules, timestamps, and lifecycle. In naming and documentation, that distinction matters because practitioners need to know where relationship facts belong.
The following SQL is illustrative and uses conventional relational constraints. The important design is the key and dependency structure, not engine-specific tuning.

codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE product (
  product_id   VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
  sku          VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  product_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE campaign (
  campaign_id   VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
  campaign_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  campaign_type VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE campaign_product (
  campaign_id  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  product_id   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  promo_price  DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  placement    VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
  unit_cap     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  selected_at  DATE NOT NULL,

  PRIMARY KEY (campaign_id, product_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (campaign_id) REFERENCES campaign (campaign_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES product (product_id),
  CHECK (promo_price >= 0),
  CHECK (unit_cap > 0)
);

sections.heading: Worked hypothetical example
paragraphs: The following small fixture is hypothetical. It is designed to show the dependency problem, not to represent a real retailer.

There are three products and two campaigns. Four relationship rows describe which products participate in which campaigns. Notice that P100 appears in both campaigns with different promotional attributes. That is valid because the relationship rows are distinct even though the product row is shared.

With this design, the product table answers product questions, the campaign table answers campaign questions, and campaign_product answers participation questions. No product attribute must be duplicated to record multiple campaigns. No campaign row needs repeating columns for an unknown number of products.

codeExamples.code:
INSERT INTO product (product_id, sku, product_name) VALUES
  ('P100', 'NB-100', 'Spiral notebook'),
  ('P200', 'PN-200', 'Blue pen pack'),
  ('P300', 'BP-300', 'Canvas backpack');

INSERT INTO campaign (campaign_id, campaign_name, campaign_type) VALUES
  ('C10', 'Back to School', 'seasonal'),
  ('C20', 'Clearance', 'markdown');

INSERT INTO campaign_product
  (campaign_id, product_id, promo_price, placement, unit_cap, selected_at)
VALUES
  ('C10', 'P100', 3.99, 'hero',      500, DATE '2026-08-01'),
  ('C10', 'P200', 0.99, 'secondary', 1000, DATE '2026-08-01'),
  ('C10', 'P300', 24.99, 'email',    200, DATE '2026-08-03'),
  ('C20', 'P100', 2.99, 'email',     150, DATE '2026-09-15');

SELECT
  c.campaign_name,
  p.product_name,
  cp.promo_price,
  cp.placement,
  cp.unit_cap
FROM campaign_product cp
JOIN campaign c ON c.campaign_id = cp.campaign_id
JOIN product p ON p.product_id = cp.product_id
ORDER BY c.campaign_id, p.product_id;

sections.heading: What the model preserves
paragraphs: The query returns four rows: Back to School with Spiral notebook at 3.99 in hero placement and cap 500; Back to School with Blue pen pack at 0.99 in secondary placement and cap 1000; Back to School with Canvas backpack at 24.99 in email placement and cap 200; and Clearance with Spiral notebook at 2.99 in email placement and cap 150.

Those results are simple, but they demonstrate the point. The same product can participate in two campaigns without duplicating the product. The same campaign can include multiple products without adding product_1, product_2, and product_3 columns. The relationship attributes are queryable because they are regular columns at the relationship grain.

Now compare a flattened product table. If product has campaign_id and promo_price columns, product P100 must either store C10 and 3.99 or C20 and 2.99. Storing both requires repeating the product row or inventing multiple campaign columns. Repeating the row means sku is no longer unique in the product table unless the model weakens a real-world product identity rule. Multiple campaign columns encode the same kind of fact in several places, which makes constraints and queries harder to reason about.

The associative entity also gives constraints a natural home. The primary key prevents the same product from being selected twice for the same campaign under the stated rule. The foreign keys prevent a campaign_product row from referring to a nonexistent campaign or product. The check constraints express local rules for relationship attributes. Database documentation for relational systems such as PostgreSQL describes these constraint types as mechanisms for enforcing table-level invariants; the modeling point is to place each invariant on the table whose grain makes it meaningful.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.product_name,
  COUNT(*) AS campaign_count,
  MIN(cp.promo_price) AS lowest_promo_price,
  MAX(cp.promo_price) AS highest_promo_price
FROM product p
JOIN campaign_product cp ON cp.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER BY p.product_id;

sections.heading: Choose the key that matches the business rule
paragraphs: The composite primary key campaign_id, product_id is correct only if a product can appear at most once in a campaign. That rule is plausible for a simple campaign selection list, but it is not universal.

If the business allows multiple offers for the same product in the same campaign, then campaign_id and product_id are not enough to identify a row. For example, a product might have separate online and in-store offers, or separate member and non-member prices. In that case, add the distinguishing attribute to the key or introduce a surrogate key while preserving a unique constraint that describes the business rule.

The key decision should be made before loading data. A surrogate key such as campaign_product_id can be useful when downstream systems need a single-column identifier or when relationship rows have their own lifecycle. But a surrogate key alone does not protect the intended grain. If the intended grain is one row per campaign, product, and channel, then a unique constraint on campaign_id, product_id, and channel is still needed. Otherwise the table permits accidental duplicates that look different only because they received different surrogate identifiers.
bullets: Use a composite key when the natural relationship grain is stable and compact.
Use a surrogate key when the relationship row needs a separate identifier, but keep a unique constraint for the real business grain.
Change the key when the business rule changes; do not hide a many-row relationship inside repeated columns.

codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE campaign_product_offer (
  campaign_product_offer_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  campaign_id  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  product_id   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  channel      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  promo_price  DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,

  UNIQUE (campaign_id, product_id, channel),
  FOREIGN KEY (campaign_id) REFERENCES campaign (campaign_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES product (product_id)
);

sections.heading: Diagnostic for practitioners
paragraphs: Use this diagnostic when reviewing an existing model with many-to-many relationships. The goal is to find facts that were flattened into the wrong entity table.

First, name the two entities independently. If each can exist without the other, they deserve separate tables. A product can exist before it appears in a campaign. A campaign can be planned before every product is selected. Their relationship is not the same thing as either entity.

Second, write a sentence for each questionable attribute. If the sentence needs both entity names, the attribute probably belongs on the associative entity. Product name belongs to product. Campaign type belongs to campaign. Promotional price for a product in a campaign belongs to campaign_product.

Third, test whether the same entity row can participate in the relationship more than once over time or across contexts. If yes, verify that the associative key includes the additional context. Otherwise the model may look normalized but still reject valid business data.

Finally, check whether downstream analytics will need to filter, group, or audit the relationship attributes. If those attributes are embedded in arrays, delimited strings, or numbered columns, normal SQL operations become awkward and constraints become weaker. The associative entity keeps the relationship visible as data rather than hiding it in column names or encoded values.
bullets: Ask whether the attribute describes an entity or a specific pairing of entities.
Reject product_1/product_2 style columns when the number of related rows is not fixed by the business.
Reject comma-separated identifiers when the relationship needs attributes, constraints, or auditability.
Document the row grain of the associative entity in one sentence before choosing keys.

takeaways: Many-to-many relationships often have their own attributes; those attributes belong on an associative entity, not arbitrarily on either parent table.
The key of the associative entity should express the relationship grain, such as one row per campaign and product, or one row per campaign, product, and channel.
Flattening a many-to-many relationship into repeated columns, delimited strings, or duplicated entity rows loses constraints and makes ordinary questions harder to answer.
A surrogate key can identify relationship rows, but it should not replace a uniqueness rule that protects the real business grain.

title: Uniqueness with nullable business identifiers
description: A practical guide to defining duplicate rules when an external business identifier is sometimes missing, using a small hypothetical customer dataset with counterexamples.
lead: Nullable business identifiers create a modeling trap: the rows with IDs and the rows without IDs do not deserve the same duplicate rule. Treat the identifier as one piece of evidence, define a separate fallback rule for missing identifiers, and keep the counterexamples visible so the rule does not silently collapse distinct customers into one record.

sections.heading: The modeling problem
paragraphs: A business identifier is an identifier assigned by a source system or business process: customer number, account number, loyalty ID, vendor code, order number, claim number, or similar. When it is present and scoped correctly, it is often the best candidate for identifying repeated observations of the same business entity. The hard case is not the identifier itself. The hard case is the nullable identifier: some rows have it, some rows do not, and the pipeline still needs a defensible duplicate rule.

The common mistake is to write one uniqueness rule for the whole table, such as “customer_id must be unique,” and then discover that many incoming records have no customer_id. Another mistake is to replace the missing identifier with a sentinel value like 'UNKNOWN' and then enforce uniqueness on that value. That does not represent the business reality. It says all customers without an external ID are the same customer, which is almost certainly false.

Relationally, NULL is not an ordinary value. In PostgreSQL’s default unique constraint behavior, null values are not considered equal to each other; PostgreSQL also documents an explicit NULLS NOT DISTINCT option for cases where a design wants nulls treated as not distinct. That distinction matters here because duplicate detection is not only a physical database feature. It is a semantic rule about whether two rows describe the same entity. If the external identifier is missing, the rule must say what evidence is strong enough to substitute for it.

A practical design separates two questions. First: when the identifier is present, what scope makes it unique? Second: when the identifier is missing, what alternate evidence is acceptable, and what evidence is only a possible match? This article uses a small hypothetical customer dataset to make those decisions concrete.

sections.heading: A hypothetical customer observation table
paragraphs: Assume a retailer receives customer observations from a web storefront and a store point-of-sale system. The target analytical model wants one customer entity, but the incoming observations are messy. The source_system column scopes identifiers because the same external_customer_id value can appear in different systems with different meanings. The example is hypothetical; it is designed to show rule behavior, not to represent actual customer data.

The proposed duplicate policy is intentionally modest. If external_customer_id is present, the duplicate key is source_system plus external_customer_id. If external_customer_id is missing, the fallback duplicate key is normalized email plus birth_date, but only when both are present. Name and postal code are not enough for automatic deduplication in this example; they are review evidence, not a unique key.

That policy is not universal. A bank, hospital, subscription business, marketplace, and retailer may all choose different fallback evidence. The important point is that the policy is explicit. It does not let NULL decide the rule accidentally.
bullets: Rule 1: Rows with a non-null external_customer_id are duplicates when they share the same source_system and external_customer_id.
Rule 2: Rows with a missing external_customer_id are duplicates when they share the same normalized email and birth_date, and both values are present.
Rule 3: Same name, same postal code, or same email alone is not enough for automatic deduplication in this hypothetical model.
Rule 4: The same external_customer_id value from two different source systems is not automatically the same customer unless the source systems share an identifier namespace.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style fixture for a hypothetical dataset.
WITH observations(obs_id, source_system, external_customer_id, email, birth_date, full_name, postal_code) AS (
  VALUES
    (1,  'web',   'W100', 'ada@example.com',   DATE '1985-04-12', 'Ada Gray',       '02139'),
    (2,  'web',   'W100', 'ada.new@example.com', DATE '1985-04-12', 'Ada Gray',     '02139'),
    (3,  'web',   NULL,   'ben@example.com',   DATE '1990-08-03', 'Ben Ito',        '94107'),
    (4,  'web',   NULL,   'BEN@example.com',   DATE '1990-08-03', 'Benjamin Ito',   '94107'),
    (5,  'web',   NULL,   NULL,                DATE '1990-08-03', 'Ben Ito',        '94107'),
    (6,  'store', NULL,   'ben@example.com',   DATE '1990-08-03', 'Ben Ito',        '94107'),
    (7,  'web',   NULL,   'chris@example.com', DATE '1988-11-20', 'Chris Lee',      '10001'),
    (8,  'web',   NULL,   'chris@example.com', DATE '1977-02-14', 'Christine Lee',  '10001'),
    (9,  'web',   'C300', 'dana@example.com',  DATE '1995-06-01', 'Dana Park',      '60601'),
    (10, 'store', 'C300', 'erik@example.com',  DATE '1982-09-09', 'Erik Stone',     '60601')
)
SELECT *
FROM observations
ORDER BY obs_id;

sections.heading: Derive two duplicate sets, not one
paragraphs: The duplicate query should reflect the two-rule design. The first branch handles rows where the source supplied an identifier. The second branch handles rows where the identifier is missing and the approved fallback evidence is complete. Keeping those branches separate prevents the common bug where rows with NULL identifiers are grouped together as if NULL were a real customer number.

The following query is illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL. It normalizes blank strings to NULL for the identifier, lowercases email for matching, and returns only groups that have more than one observation. The expected output is shown after the query.

The expected duplicate groups are easy to verify from the fixture. Observations 1 and 2 share web:W100, so they are duplicates under the external ID rule even though their email values differ. Observations 3, 4, and 6 have no external ID and share ben@example.com plus 1990-08-03 after email normalization, so they are duplicates under the fallback rule. Observation 5 looks similar to Ben Ito but lacks email, so it does not meet the fallback key. Observations 7 and 8 share email but have different birth dates, so email alone is not sufficient. Observations 9 and 10 share the literal value C300, but their source systems differ, so they are not duplicates under the external ID rule.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style duplicate diagnostic.
WITH observations(obs_id, source_system, external_customer_id, email, birth_date, full_name, postal_code) AS (
  VALUES
    (1,  'web',   'W100', 'ada@example.com',     DATE '1985-04-12', 'Ada Gray',       '02139'),
    (2,  'web',   'W100', 'ada.new@example.com', DATE '1985-04-12', 'Ada Gray',       '02139'),
    (3,  'web',   NULL,   'ben@example.com',     DATE '1990-08-03', 'Ben Ito',        '94107'),
    (4,  'web',   NULL,   'BEN@example.com',     DATE '1990-08-03', 'Benjamin Ito',   '94107'),
    (5,  'web',   NULL,   NULL,                  DATE '1990-08-03', 'Ben Ito',        '94107'),
    (6,  'store', NULL,   'ben@example.com',     DATE '1990-08-03', 'Ben Ito',        '94107'),
    (7,  'web',   NULL,   'chris@example.com',   DATE '1988-11-20', 'Chris Lee',      '10001'),
    (8,  'web',   NULL,   'chris@example.com',   DATE '1977-02-14', 'Christine Lee',  '10001'),
    (9,  'web',   'C300', 'dana@example.com',    DATE '1995-06-01', 'Dana Park',      '60601'),
    (10, 'store', 'C300', 'erik@example.com',    DATE '1982-09-09', 'Erik Stone',     '60601')
),
normalized AS (
  SELECT
    obs_id,
    source_system,
    NULLIF(TRIM(external_customer_id), '') AS ext_id,
    LOWER(NULLIF(TRIM(email), '')) AS email_norm,
    birth_date,
    full_name,
    postal_code
  FROM observations
),
external_id_duplicates AS (
  SELECT
    'external_id_present' AS rule_name,
    source_system || ':' || ext_id AS duplicate_key,
    ARRAY_AGG(obs_id ORDER BY obs_id) AS observation_ids
  FROM normalized
  WHERE ext_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY source_system, ext_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
),
missing_id_fallback_duplicates AS (
  SELECT
    'missing_external_fallback' AS rule_name,
    email_norm || '|' || birth_date::text AS duplicate_key,
    ARRAY_AGG(obs_id ORDER BY obs_id) AS observation_ids
  FROM normalized
  WHERE ext_id IS NULL
    AND email_norm IS NOT NULL
    AND birth_date IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY email_norm, birth_date
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
)
SELECT * FROM external_id_duplicates
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM missing_id_fallback_duplicates
ORDER BY rule_name, duplicate_key;

sections.heading: Expected result and counterexamples
paragraphs: The diagnostic should return two groups: external_id_present with key web:W100 and observation IDs 1 and 2, and missing_external_fallback with key ben@example.com|1990-08-03 and observation IDs 3, 4, and 6. Those are the only automatic duplicate groups under the stated policy.

The counterexamples are as important as the matches. Observation 5 has the same name, birth date, and postal code as Ben Ito, but it has no email and no external ID. If the model automatically merged it into the Ben group, it would be using name and postal code as part of the actual duplicate rule despite saying otherwise. That may be a valid business decision in some domains, but it should not happen by accident.

Observations 7 and 8 show why a fallback key should not be weakened silently. They share chris@example.com, but their birth dates differ. This could be a shared inbox, a recycled address, a typo, a household account, or two records that need manual review. The point is not that they can never be the same person. The point is that they do not meet the automatic duplicate rule.

Observations 9 and 10 show the identifier-scope problem. Both contain external_customer_id C300, but one came from web and one came from store. If identifiers are source-scoped, then C300 is not a complete key by itself. The duplicate key must include source_system. If the business later establishes that web and store share a global customer namespace, the rule can change, but the model should not assume that from the raw value alone.
bullets: Automatic duplicate: rows 1 and 2, because source_system plus external_customer_id is web:W100.
Automatic duplicate: rows 3, 4, and 6, because external_customer_id is missing and normalized email plus birth_date matches.
Not automatic duplicate: row 5 with rows 3, 4, or 6, because the fallback key is incomplete.
Not automatic duplicate: rows 7 and 8, because email matches but birth_date does not.
Not automatic duplicate: rows 9 and 10, because the external identifier value is the same but the source scope differs.

sections.heading: Choosing the fallback key
paragraphs: A fallback key is not a consolation prize for a missing ID. It is an alternate candidate for identifying the entity under clearly stated assumptions. The assumptions should be written down next to the rule because future maintainers will otherwise reinterpret the rule from the SQL alone.

For the hypothetical retailer, email plus birth_date is treated as strong enough for automatic deduplication only when both values are present. That choice assumes email is collected reliably enough, birth date is not usually fabricated, and the cost of failing to merge some true duplicates is lower than the cost of merging distinct people. In another domain, email may be weak evidence. In a business-to-business model, a shared billing email may represent an organization rather than a person. In a family retail account, multiple people may share one address. The fallback key should match the entity being modeled.

A good fallback rule also states what to do with partial evidence. Missing email does not mean “use name instead” unless the policy says so. Different birth dates do not mean “ignore birth date because email matches” unless the policy says so. If the team wants possible-match review queues, define them separately from automatic duplicate groups.

One useful pattern is a three-tier outcome: match, possible match, and no match. Match rules are safe enough for automatic consolidation. Possible-match rules create review candidates or downstream quality metrics. No-match cases remain separate. This pattern keeps the customer dimension from being over-merged while still surfacing records that deserve attention.
bullets: State the entity: customer, account, household, organization, device, order, or event.
State the identifier namespace: global, source-scoped, tenant-scoped, region-scoped, or time-scoped.
State the present-ID rule separately from the missing-ID rule.
Require complete fallback evidence for automatic deduplication.
Keep weaker evidence in a possible-match rule rather than pretending it is a key.

sections.heading: A decision template for nullable identifiers
paragraphs: When a source identifier is nullable, define the duplicate policy before writing the constraint, merge, or validation query. The policy can be short, but it should answer the questions that determine whether two rows describe the same entity.

The template below is intentionally relational rather than tool-specific. It can inform a database constraint, a dbt test, an ingestion validation, a reconciliation query, or a stewardship workflow. The implementation choice is separate from the semantic decision.

The key discipline is to avoid mixing rows with identifiers and rows without identifiers into a single vague rule. Rows with identifiers can usually be matched on the identifier’s declared scope. Rows without identifiers need a fallback candidate key. Rows with weak or incomplete evidence need a review category, not a hidden merge.
bullets: Entity: What real-world thing does one row attempt to describe?
Grain: Is each row an observation, the current state of an entity, or a historical version?
Identifier scope: Is the external identifier unique globally or only within a source, tenant, region, or time period?
Present-ID rule: Which columns form the duplicate key when the external identifier is present?
Missing-ID rule: Which alternate columns form the duplicate key when the external identifier is missing?
Completeness requirement: Which fallback columns must be non-null before the fallback rule can fire?
Conflict handling: Which attributes may differ inside a duplicate group without breaking identity?
Possible-match rule: Which weaker similarities should be reviewed but not automatically merged?
Counterexamples: Which plausible-looking pairs are explicitly not duplicates?

sections.heading: What not to do
paragraphs: Do not coalesce missing identifiers to a single value such as 'UNKNOWN' and then treat that expression as a unique business key. That makes every missing identifier collide with every other missing identifier. It is useful only if the business truly believes all missing-ID rows are the same entity, which is rarely the case.

Do not rely on a database’s default NULL behavior as the whole duplicate policy. Multiple NULLs may be allowed by a unique constraint, but “allowed to coexist” is not the same as “known to be distinct.” Conversely, forcing nulls to compare as not distinct can be valid for some constraints but is usually wrong for external customer IDs because it treats absence of evidence as a shared identifier.

Do not let the fallback rule grow informally. If the first version says email plus birth date, then a later change to email plus name is not a harmless refactor; it changes which people can be merged. Treat that as a data modeling decision, with new counterexamples and expected results.

Finally, do not erase the distinction between automatic matches and review candidates. A possible match can be extremely useful for data quality work, but it is not the same thing as a duplicate key. The model should preserve that difference.

takeaways: Rows with a present external identifier and rows with a missing external identifier need separate duplicate rules.
NULL should not be converted into a fake shared business identifier; missing evidence is not identity evidence.
A fallback key must state its required columns, its assumptions, and its counterexamples.
Identifier scope matters: the same external ID value may or may not be unique across source systems.
Keep possible matches separate from automatic duplicate groups so weak evidence does not silently merge distinct entities.

title: Domain constraints for categorical data
description: A practical guide to choosing controlled vocabularies for categorical data while keeping unknown, invalid, and not-applicable values separate.
lead: Domain constraints for categorical data are not just a way to reject misspellings. They are a way to state what an attribute is allowed to mean. The hard part is choosing a controlled vocabulary without turning missing evidence into a fake category or accepting invalid source values because they are convenient to store.

sections.heading: The modeling problem
paragraphs: A categorical column looks simple until the source system sends values that do not fit the intended meaning. A retail order status might arrive as paid, CANCELLED, null, shippped, or BACKORDERED. Only some of those are valid order statuses. One is missing. One is a typo. One may describe inventory availability rather than the order lifecycle.

The common mistake is to add every observed string to the controlled vocabulary. That keeps the load green, but it makes the model worse. Reports can no longer tell whether backordered means an order status, a fulfillment state, or an exception that needs mapping. A second mistake is to add unknown to the domain of order statuses. Unknown is usually not a business state of the order. It is a statement about the data warehouse's current knowledge.

A better design separates three concepts. Valid values are members of the domain for the attribute. Unknown means the attribute may have a valid value, but it was not provided or not yet derived. Invalid means an observed value does not belong to the domain as defined. Not applicable means the attribute does not apply to this entity at this grain. These distinctions should be visible in the schema and in the load diagnostics.

sections.heading: A hypothetical order fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order feed. The analytical table needs an order_status_code at the order grain. The business question is narrow: where is the order in its commercial lifecycle? For this example, the approved status domain is placed, paid, fulfilled, or cancelled.

The source feed contains five rows. Order 201 sends PAID, which can map to paid. Order 202 sends no status. Order 203 sends shippped, which is not a member of the domain and is probably a source typo. Order 204 sends BACKORDERED, which is a real operational condition but not an order lifecycle status in this model. Order 205 sends CANCELLED, which can map to cancelled.

The expected result is three accepted canonical rows and two exception rows. Orders 201 and 205 are known. Order 202 is accepted with no status code and a knowledge state of unknown_from_source. Orders 203 and 204 are not silently converted into domain values. They are exceptions: one because the raw value is invalid, the other because it appears to answer a different attribute question.
This is the key modeling move: the controlled vocabulary is chosen from the meaning of the attribute, not from the union of strings observed in a source column.
bullets: Valid domain for order_status_code: placed, paid, fulfilled, cancelled.
Unknown example: order 202 has no source value, so the warehouse does not know the status yet.
Invalid example: shippped is an observed value but not a valid domain member.
Wrong-attribute example: BACKORDERED may belong to inventory_commitment_status, not order_status_code.

sections.heading: An illustrative relational design
paragraphs: The following SQL is illustrative for PostgreSQL 18 syntax. It is not presented as executed benchmark or deployment evidence. The important relational idea is portable: use the domain table or constraint to define valid values, and use a separate column or exception table to describe knowledge about the value.

The status domain table contains only valid order statuses. The canonical order table permits a null status only when the knowledge state says the value is unknown from the source. It does not permit a known row without a status code, and it does not permit a status code on an unknown row. Invalid raw values belong in a staging or exception structure, not in the trusted domain.

sections.heading: Worked load classification
paragraphs: A load step needs to classify the staged values before they reach the canonical table. The raw-to-canonical mapping is deliberately smaller than the set of observed raw strings. PAID and CANCELLED are recognized aliases. A null raw value is unknown. shippped is not recognized. BACKORDERED is treated as a counterexample: it should not be added to order_status_code merely because it appears in the same source field.

The classification below has five input rows. The expected counts are: known equals 2, unknown_from_source equals 1, and exception equals 2. Those counts add back to the five staged rows, which is a useful reconciliation check.

codeExamples.code:
WITH staged_order(order_id, raw_order_status) AS (
    VALUES
        (201, 'PAID'),
        (202, NULL),
        (203, 'shippped'),
        (204, 'BACKORDERED'),
        (205, 'CANCELLED')
),
raw_status_alias(raw_value, status_code) AS (
    VALUES
        ('PAID', 'paid'),
        ('CANCELLED', 'cancelled')
),
classified AS (
    SELECT
        s.order_id,
        s.raw_order_status,
        a.status_code,
        CASE
            WHEN s.raw_order_status IS NULL THEN 'unknown_from_source'
            WHEN a.status_code IS NOT NULL THEN 'known'
            WHEN s.raw_order_status = 'BACKORDERED' THEN 'wrong_attribute_question'
            ELSE 'invalid_raw_value'
        END AS classification
    FROM staged_order s
    LEFT JOIN raw_status_alias a
        ON s.raw_order_status = a.raw_value
)
SELECT classification, count(*) AS row_count
FROM classified
GROUP BY classification
ORDER BY classification;

sections.heading: How to choose the controlled vocabulary
paragraphs: Start by writing the attribute question in one sentence. For the example, the question is: what is the order's commercial lifecycle status? That sentence excludes values that answer adjacent questions, such as whether inventory is backordered, whether a package is damaged, or whether payment is at risk. Those may be valid attributes, but they are not values of this attribute.

Next, decide whether a proposed value is a real business state or a data state. paid is a business state. unknown_from_source is a data state. Treating unknown as an order status would let analysts count unknown orders as if the orders had intentionally entered an unknown lifecycle state. That is rarely what the business means.

Then decide how the model should behave when the value arrives late. In dimensional models, late-arriving descriptive context is a known pattern: facts may be loaded before all dimensional context is available. The same principle applies here. A missing status can be represented as unknown knowledge temporarily, then updated when a valid status is obtained. That is different from promoting unknown into the status domain.

Finally, define where invalid observations go. A strict relational design can reject them from the trusted table and store them in an exception table with the raw value. A more permissive landing layer can store every raw value, but the curated layer should still prevent invalid values from masquerading as members of the controlled vocabulary.
bullets: If the value describes the entity's real state, consider it for the domain.
If the value describes what the warehouse does not know, model it as knowledge or quality metadata.
If the value is observed but outside the definition, route it to an exception path.
If the value answers another question, create or use the correct attribute instead of overloading this one.

sections.heading: Diagnostics that protect semantics
paragraphs: A domain constraint is incomplete without a diagnostic that tells operators what happened to source values. The minimum diagnostic should reconcile staged rows to accepted known rows, accepted unknown rows, and exception rows. If those categories do not add back to the staged count, the load logic has lost or duplicated records.

Another useful diagnostic is the raw-value frequency report for exceptions. If shippped appears once, it may be a source typo. If it appears thousands of times, it may indicate a new source-system code or a mapping gap. Either way, the response is not to blindly add shippped to the domain. The response is to decide whether it maps to an existing valid status, represents a new valid status, or belongs to another attribute.

The model should also make downstream filtering explicit. An analyst asking for paid orders should filter order_status_code = paid. An analyst measuring data completeness should filter status_knowledge = unknown_from_source or inspect the exception table. Those are different questions, and the schema should not force both questions through the same categorical column.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative reconciliation expectation for the hypothetical fixture:
-- staged rows: 5
-- accepted known rows: 2
-- accepted unknown rows: 1
-- exception rows: 2
-- 2 + 1 + 2 = 5

SELECT raw_order_status, count(*) AS exception_count
FROM order_status_exception
GROUP BY raw_order_status
ORDER BY exception_count DESC, raw_order_status;

sections.heading: The practical rule
paragraphs: A controlled vocabulary should contain the valid answers to one attribute question. It should not contain every string the source has emitted, and it should not contain placeholders for the warehouse's lack of knowledge unless the business truly has such a state.

Use constraints to make the intended meaning hard to violate. A foreign key to a domain table or a check constraint can enforce membership in the valid set. A separate knowledge-state column, staging table, or exception table can preserve the difference between unknown and invalid. This keeps the model honest: valid values support analysis, unknown values measure incompleteness, and invalid values drive remediation.

The payoff is semantic stability. When the vocabulary is chosen this way, adding a new value becomes a modeling decision rather than an ingestion reflex. The team can ask: is this a valid state of the attribute, a missing value, a bad value, or a value for a different attribute? That question is the center of domain constraints for categorical data.

takeaways: Choose categorical domain values from the meaning of the attribute, not from every raw string observed in a source feed.
Model unknown as a knowledge state when the value is missing or late; do not turn it into a fake business category.
Route invalid or wrong-attribute values to an exception path so they can be corrected, mapped, or modeled separately.
Use relational constraints to protect the curated layer, and use diagnostics to reconcile known, unknown, and exception counts.

title: Relational division for analytical questions
description: A practical guide to using relational division to find entities that satisfy every requirement in a reference set, with a hypothetical retail example and counterexamples.
lead: Many analytical questions are not asking whether an entity matched one condition. They are asking whether it matched every condition in a reference set. Relational division is the relational pattern behind that question: find the rows on the left whose related rows cover all rows on the right.

sections.heading: The shape of the question
paragraphs: Relational division is useful when the requirement is universal: all required products, all required documents, all required onboarding steps, all required permissions, or all required data quality checks. In data engineering work, this often appears as an eligibility question: which customers completed every required action, which stores stocked every item in an assortment, or which accounts have every mandatory configuration flag enabled?

The trap is that many queries answer a weaker question. A join can tell you who matched at least one requirement. A count of events can tell you who did enough things, but not necessarily the right things. Relational division asks whether the set of facts for one entity contains the whole reference set.

In relational terms, imagine a relation R(entity_id, requirement_id) and a reference relation S(requirement_id). The division-like question is: which entity_id values in R are associated with every requirement_id in S? SQL does not usually expose a division operator directly, but the logic can be written with anti-joins, NOT EXISTS, or grouped aggregation.

This article uses a small hypothetical retail dataset. The goal is to find customers who purchased every SKU required for a campaign bundle. The pattern generalizes, but the example stays small enough to inspect manually.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Assume a campaign called fall-kit requires three SKUs: beans, coffee-filter, and mug. A customer qualifies only if their distinct purchased SKU set includes all three. Extra purchases do not disqualify them. Duplicate purchases should not help them pretend they purchased a missing SKU.

The following SQL fixture is illustrative. It uses common table expressions and VALUES to make the example self-contained. The expected qualifying customers are c01 and c04. Customer c01 bought all three required SKUs and one extra SKU. Customer c04 bought all three required SKUs, including a duplicate beans event. Customer c02 is missing mug. Customer c03 bought mug twice and beans once, but is missing coffee-filter. Customer c05 bought only a non-required SKU.
bullets: c01 qualifies: beans, coffee-filter, and mug are all present; spoon is irrelevant.
c02 does not qualify: beans and coffee-filter are present, but mug is missing.
c03 does not qualify: duplicate mug does not replace the missing coffee-filter.
c04 qualifies: all three required SKUs are present; duplicate beans is harmless after deduplication.
c05 does not qualify: tea is not part of the required set.

codeExamples.code:
WITH required_campaign_sku(campaign_id, sku) AS (
    VALUES
        ('fall-kit', 'beans'),
        ('fall-kit', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('fall-kit', 'mug')
),
customer_sku_event(customer_id, sku) AS (
    VALUES
        ('c01', 'beans'),
        ('c01', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c01', 'mug'),
        ('c01', 'spoon'),
        ('c02', 'beans'),
        ('c02', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c03', 'mug'),
        ('c03', 'mug'),
        ('c03', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c04', 'mug'),
        ('c05', 'tea')
)
SELECT *
FROM required_campaign_sku;

-- Expected required SKUs for fall-kit:
-- beans
-- coffee-filter
-- mug

sections.heading: Relational division with double NOT EXISTS
paragraphs: A reliable way to express relational division in SQL is to ask for entities for which no missing requirement exists. That sentence is easier to reason about than it first appears. A customer qualifies when there does not exist a required SKU for which there does not exist a matching customer purchase.

This is sometimes called a double negative pattern. The outer NOT EXISTS rejects customers with at least one missing requirement. The inner NOT EXISTS detects the missing requirement for the current customer. The result is the set of customers whose facts cover the complete reference set.

The query below first deduplicates customer and SKU pairs. This is not just cosmetic. The logical relation for the division question is customer-to-SKU coverage, not purchase events. If a customer bought mug twice, the second mug should not change coverage. In a warehouse, this deduplicated relation might be a modeled bridge table, a distinct projection over events, or a materialized eligibility input.

codeExamples.code:
WITH required_campaign_sku(campaign_id, sku) AS (
    VALUES
        ('fall-kit', 'beans'),
        ('fall-kit', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('fall-kit', 'mug')
),
customer_sku_event(customer_id, sku) AS (
    VALUES
        ('c01', 'beans'),
        ('c01', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c01', 'mug'),
        ('c01', 'spoon'),
        ('c02', 'beans'),
        ('c02', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c03', 'mug'),
        ('c03', 'mug'),
        ('c03', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c04', 'mug'),
        ('c05', 'tea')
),
customer_sku AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, sku
    FROM customer_sku_event
),
candidate_customer AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
    FROM customer_sku_event
)
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM candidate_customer AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM required_campaign_sku AS r
    WHERE r.campaign_id = 'fall-kit'
      AND NOT EXISTS (
          SELECT 1
          FROM customer_sku AS p
          WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
            AND p.sku = r.sku
      )
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

-- Expected result:
-- c01
-- c04

sections.heading: Why not just count events?
paragraphs: A common counterexample is a query that counts purchase events and compares the count to the number of requirements. That query is wrong because event count is not set coverage. Customer c03 has three purchase events in the fixture: mug, mug, and beans. The fall-kit campaign has three required SKUs. A naive event-count query can incorrectly qualify c03 even though coffee-filter is missing.

The fix is not merely to count more carefully. The fix is to align the grain of the query with the logical question. The question is about distinct customer-to-required-SKU coverage. That means duplicates must collapse, non-required SKUs must not inflate the count, and the denominator must be the number of required SKUs in the reference set.

Grouped aggregation can express the same division logic when the reference set is non-empty and the requirement key is unique. It is often compact and readable. Join customer coverage to the required set, group by customer, and require the number of distinct matched required SKUs to equal the number of required SKUs. The join removes non-required SKUs; COUNT(DISTINCT) prevents duplicate purchases from inflating the numerator.

The aggregation form is useful, but it has a different edge-case shape from the double NOT EXISTS form. If the reference set is empty, pure relational logic says every candidate entity satisfies every requirement, because there is no requirement to violate. Some business questions want that vacuous truth; others want no one to qualify until at least one requirement exists. Decide this explicitly instead of leaving it as an accidental behavior.

codeExamples.code:
WITH required_campaign_sku(campaign_id, sku) AS (
    VALUES
        ('fall-kit', 'beans'),
        ('fall-kit', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('fall-kit', 'mug')
),
customer_sku_event(customer_id, sku) AS (
    VALUES
        ('c01', 'beans'),
        ('c01', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c01', 'mug'),
        ('c01', 'spoon'),
        ('c02', 'beans'),
        ('c02', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c03', 'mug'),
        ('c03', 'mug'),
        ('c03', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'beans'),
        ('c04', 'coffee-filter'),
        ('c04', 'mug'),
        ('c05', 'tea')
),
customer_sku AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, sku
    FROM customer_sku_event
),
required_count AS (
    SELECT campaign_id, COUNT(*) AS required_sku_count
    FROM required_campaign_sku
    WHERE campaign_id = 'fall-kit'
    GROUP BY campaign_id
)
SELECT p.customer_id
FROM customer_sku AS p
JOIN required_campaign_sku AS r
  ON r.sku = p.sku
 AND r.campaign_id = 'fall-kit'
CROSS JOIN required_count AS rc
GROUP BY p.customer_id, rc.required_sku_count
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.sku) = rc.required_sku_count
ORDER BY p.customer_id;

-- Expected result:
-- c01
-- c04

sections.heading: Modeling assumptions that matter
paragraphs: Relational division depends on the reference set being well defined. If required_campaign_sku contains duplicate rows for the same campaign and SKU, then the requirement set is ambiguous. A candidate key such as campaign_id plus sku is the natural way to state that each required SKU appears at most once per campaign. In SQL databases, primary key or unique constraints are the usual mechanisms for enforcing that kind of rule.

The fact side also needs a clear grain. In the fixture, customer_sku_event represents events, not coverage. Multiple events can map to the same customer and SKU. The division query therefore uses a distinct projection named customer_sku. If the warehouse already has a bridge table at the coverage grain, that table should have a key or uniqueness rule matching its intended grain.

Nulls deserve special care. A null SKU in either the required set or the customer coverage set is not a normal requirement identifier. For this pattern, requirement identifiers should be known, comparable values. If the business needs to represent unknown or invalid product codes, model that separately rather than letting null semantics decide eligibility.

The candidate entity set is another explicit choice. The double NOT EXISTS example draws candidates from customers with at least one purchase event. If the business wants to consider all registered customers, including customers with no purchases, candidate_customer should come from the customer dimension instead. That distinction matters most when the requirement set is empty or when eligibility reports must show non-qualifying customers.
bullets: Give the reference relation a key at the requirement grain, such as campaign_id and sku.
Deduplicate event data before asking a set coverage question.
Choose the candidate entity population intentionally; do not let it be an accidental side effect of the fact table.
Define how the query should behave when the reference set is empty.
Keep requirement identifiers non-null for the division comparison.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative table design for the reference set.
-- Constraint syntax varies by database, but the modeling point is durable:
-- one row per campaign requirement.
CREATE TABLE required_campaign_sku (
    campaign_id text NOT NULL,
    sku text NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (campaign_id, sku)
);

-- Event data may contain repeated customer/SKU pairs because events are not coverage.
CREATE TABLE customer_sku_event (
    event_id text PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id text NOT NULL,
    sku text NOT NULL
);

-- Coverage can be derived when asking the division question.
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, sku
FROM customer_sku_event;

sections.heading: A diagnostic for analytical reviews
paragraphs: When reviewing an eligibility query, start by naming the entity, the requirement set, and the evidence relation. For the fixture, the entity is customer, the requirement set is fall-kit SKUs, and the evidence relation is distinct customer-to-SKU coverage. If those three nouns are not clear, the query is likely to drift into counting events or matching any row.

Next, create counterexamples on purpose. Include an entity with all requirements, an entity with one missing requirement, an entity with duplicate evidence for one requirement, and an entity with extra irrelevant evidence. These rows make it difficult for an incorrect query to pass unnoticed. In the fixture, c03 is the important counterexample because it exposes the difference between event count and requirement coverage.

Finally, inspect the denominator. The denominator should come from the reference relation, not from the candidate entity’s facts. If the question is every required SKU in fall-kit, the count of required SKUs is determined by required_campaign_sku for fall-kit. A query that lets each customer’s purchases define the denominator is not answering the universal question.

The practical rule is simple: if the English sentence contains “every,” “all,” “complete,” or “missing none,” look for relational division. Then decide whether the clearest expression is double NOT EXISTS or grouped aggregation. The right choice is the one that preserves the semantics under duplicates, irrelevant facts, and the expected empty-set behavior.

takeaways: Relational division answers universal analytical questions: find entities whose related facts cover every row in a reference set.
A join alone usually answers “matched at least one,” not “matched all.” Use double NOT EXISTS or grouped aggregation to express full coverage.
Counterexamples with duplicates, missing requirements, and extra irrelevant facts are the fastest way to validate the query’s semantics.
The reference set needs a clear key, and event facts often need to be deduplicated to the coverage grain before division logic is applied.
Decide empty-reference-set behavior explicitly because mathematical vacuous truth may not match the business rule.

title: Temporal uniqueness constraints
description: A practical guide to deciding when two records may share the same identifier across time, using a hypothetical customer loyalty dataset with counterexamples.
lead: A normal uniqueness constraint answers a static question: can two rows in this table have the same value right now? A temporal uniqueness constraint answers a different question: can two rows use the same identifier during overlapping periods of validity? That difference matters when identifiers are reassigned, corrected, scoped by market, or represented as history instead of current state.

sections.heading: The question temporal uniqueness answers
paragraphs: A candidate key says that a set of attributes uniquely identifies a row in a relation. For a current-state table, that is often enough. If a loyalty number identifies one active customer, a conventional uniqueness rule over loyalty_number may be correct.

History changes the meaning of uniqueness. Suppose a retailer allows a loyalty number to be retired and later reassigned. A rule that says loyalty_number must be unique forever is too strict. A rule that says loyalty_number plus valid_from must be unique is too weak, because it permits two active assignments with different start dates. The missing concept is overlap.

A temporal uniqueness constraint can be stated in relational terms: within a chosen scope, two distinct records may share an identifier only when their validity intervals do not overlap. The important words are scope, identifier, and validity interval. If any of those are vague, the constraint will either reject legitimate history or allow ambiguous facts.

This article uses valid time: the period when the modeled fact is true in the business domain. That is separate from transaction time, which records when the database learned or changed a fact. If a table mixes valid-time history with correction history, uniqueness rules become hard to reason about because duplicate rows may mean either an actual business overlap or a later correction.
bullets: Scope: the attributes that define the namespace of the identifier, such as market, tenant, brand, or source system.
Identifier: the value being constrained, such as loyalty number, subscription ID, device ID, or contract number.
Validity interval: the period during which the row claims the identifier is assigned to the entity.

sections.heading: A hypothetical loyalty example with counterexamples
paragraphs: Assume a hypothetical retail company assigns loyalty numbers to customers. The business rule is: within one market, a loyalty number can identify at most one customer at any instant. The same loyalty number can be reused after the previous assignment ends. The same printed number may also exist in different markets, so market is part of the identifier scope.

Use half-open intervals: valid_from is inclusive and valid_to is exclusive. In other words, the interval 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-01 covers the start of January 1 through just before March 1. This convention makes back-to-back assignments easy to evaluate because one row can end on the same instant another begins without overlap.
The following fixture is hypothetical. It is small enough to evaluate by inspection, but it contains the cases that usually expose an incomplete model.
bullets: Rows 1 and 2 share loyalty number L100 in the US, but row 1 ends exactly when row 2 begins. Under the half-open convention, they do not overlap, so they are allowed.
Rows 3 and 4 share loyalty number L200 in the US and overlap from 2026-02-01 through just before 2026-02-15. They violate the rule.

Rows 5 and 6 share loyalty number L300 in the US for the same customer. They still overlap. If this table represents valid assignments, the duplicate is ambiguous and should be rejected or modeled as a correction elsewhere.
Rows 1 and 7 share loyalty number L100 during February, but row 7 is in CA. If market is truly part of the namespace, they are allowed. If loyalty numbers are global, they are not allowed.

sections.heading: Why ordinary keys are not enough
paragraphs: A static key chooses one of two bad answers for this example. A unique constraint on market and loyalty_number prevents reassignment, so it rejects rows 1 and 2 even though the business allows reuse after termination. A unique constraint on market, loyalty_number, and valid_from accepts rows 3 and 4, because their start dates differ, even though the records overlap and create two customers for the same loyalty number at the same time.

The temporal rule is not about whether a single column repeats. It is about whether two facts can both be true at the same instant. That is why temporal uniqueness is closer to a mutual-exclusion rule than to a conventional candidate key.

The precise overlap test for half-open intervals is: interval A overlaps interval B when A starts before B ends and B starts before A ends. With open-ended current rows, null valid_to needs a declared meaning. In this article, null valid_to means the assignment continues indefinitely. A production model might instead use a non-null high date or a native range type, but the semantic rule is the same.

Be careful with null identifiers. If the value is unknown, it is usually not an identifier yet. Allowing many null loyalty numbers may be fine, but it is not evidence that several records share the same identifier. Treat unknown, not applicable, and invalid as separate modeling cases rather than relying on accidental database behavior around nulls.

sections.heading: A diagnostic query for existing data
paragraphs: The following illustrative SQL is a diagnostic, not a claim that it was executed. It searches for pairs of rows that violate the stated rule in the hypothetical fixture. It treats null valid_to as an open-ended interval by substituting a high date for comparison.

For the fixture above, the expected violating pairs are assignment 3 with 4, and assignment 5 with 6. Pair 1 with 2 is not returned because the intervals only touch at the boundary. Pair 1 with 7 is not returned because market is part of the scope.

The diagnostic is useful before choosing an enforcement mechanism. If it returns rows, the team must decide whether the data is wrong, the scope is wrong, or the table is mixing different kinds of history. Do not add a constraint until that decision is explicit; otherwise the constraint may simply formalize the wrong rule.

codeExamples.code:
select
    a.assignment_id as left_assignment_id,
    b.assignment_id as right_assignment_id,
    a.market,
    a.loyalty_number,
    greatest(a.valid_from, b.valid_from) as overlap_starts_at,
    least(
        coalesce(a.valid_to, date '9999-12-31'),
        coalesce(b.valid_to, date '9999-12-31')
    ) as overlap_ends_before
from loyalty_assignment a
join loyalty_assignment b
  on a.assignment_id < b.assignment_id
 and a.market = b.market
 and a.loyalty_number = b.loyalty_number
 and a.valid_from < coalesce(b.valid_to, date '9999-12-31')
 and b.valid_from < coalesce(a.valid_to, date '9999-12-31')
order by a.assignment_id, b.assignment_id;

sections.heading: Turning the rule into a modeling decision
paragraphs: The constraint should be written as a business sentence before it is written as DDL: within market, loyalty_number identifies at most one customer during any instant of valid time. That sentence is compact, but it contains several decisions.

First, choose the namespace. In the example, market is part of the scope. If the same loyalty number cannot exist in two countries at the same time, remove market from the scope. If each tenant, brand, or source system owns its own numbering scheme, include that attribute. Most accidental temporal uniqueness bugs come from leaving the namespace implicit.

Second, choose the interval convention. Half-open intervals are often easier to maintain than closed intervals because adjacency is unambiguous. With closed intervals, a row ending on March 1 and another starting on March 1 overlap at March 1. That may or may not be intended. The data model should not leave that to interpretation.

Third, choose the time basis. If assignments are recorded as instants, define the clock and time zone rules. For analytics, dimensional modeling guidance often recommends preserving useful local-time context while also standardizing time for comparison. The core temporal uniqueness rule still needs one comparable timeline for overlap checks.

Fourth, decide whether same-entity overlap is allowed. In the hypothetical fixture, rows 5 and 6 overlap for the same customer. Some teams are tempted to allow that because no second customer is involved. But if both rows represent the same valid assignment, the overlap is still a duplicate assertion. If one row is a superseded correction, model correction history separately, for example with transaction-time columns or a separate audit table.
bullets: If the business says an identifier is never reused, use ordinary uniqueness over the identifier scope instead of temporal uniqueness.
If the business says an identifier can be reused only after expiration, use temporal uniqueness over the identifier scope and validity interval.
If the business says simultaneous sharing is legitimate, the value is not a unique identifier for that entity at that time; model it as a contact value, label, or relationship instead.
If the business needs both valid-time history and correction history, do not overload one interval to mean both.

sections.heading: Enforcement options and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Relational databases differ in how directly they can enforce temporal uniqueness. PostgreSQL documentation describes ordinary unique constraints, check constraints, and exclusion constraints; exclusion constraints are one way to express that certain combinations, such as equal identifiers with overlapping ranges, must not coexist. This article does not depend on a specific implementation choice, because the modeling rule is independent of the engine.

There are three common enforcement patterns. The first is a native database constraint, when the engine can express equality on the scope and non-overlap on the period. This keeps bad data out at write time. The second is a transactionally safe application or stored-procedure check. This can work, but it must handle concurrent writes or two overlapping assignments may be inserted at the same time. The third is a batch data quality diagnostic, which is useful in warehouses and lakehouses but detects violations after they arrive.

The tradeoff is not just performance. It is also where the organization wants the rule to live. If downstream reporting assumes one customer per loyalty number per instant, the rule belongs as close to the authoritative assignment table as possible. If the table is a raw event log, then temporal uniqueness may belong in a curated table that interprets events as assignment intervals.

The modeling test is simple: ask whether two rows with the same scoped identifier can both be true for the same instant. If yes, the identifier is not unique for that entity at that time. If no, write the non-overlap rule explicitly and make every exception name a different scope, a different interval, or a different kind of history.

takeaways: Temporal uniqueness means a scoped identifier may repeat across rows only when the rows' validity intervals do not overlap.
A static unique key can be too strict for reassignment or too weak for overlapping history; the overlap rule is the essential part.
Define scope, interval convention, open-ended intervals, and correction history before choosing an enforcement mechanism.
A small counterexample dataset can reveal whether the intended rule allows boundary-touching, cross-scope reuse, same-entity duplicates, and open-ended current records.

title: Floating-point error in financial analytics
description: A practitioner guide to demonstrating representation error in repeated decimal arithmetic, with a hypothetical retail coupon example and diagnostic rules for aggregates.
lead: Financial analytics often repeats small decimal amounts: fees, discounts, credits, tax-like adjustments, loyalty points converted to currency, or per-event revenue allocations. If those decimals are represented as binary floating-point values, the stored value may not equal the decimal value analysts intend. This article shows how to demonstrate the error with explicit arithmetic, without relying on a particular runtime’s printed output.

sections.heading: Why repeated decimals are the problem
paragraphs: The practical issue is not that computers sometimes make mysterious arithmetic mistakes. The issue is representation. A finite binary floating-point value is a rational number whose denominator is a power of two. In simplified form, it looks like k divided by 2^n for some integers k and n. Many ordinary financial decimals do not have that form.

Consider 0.10 dollars. As a fraction, 0.10 is 1/10. If 1/10 could be represented exactly as k/2^n, then 1/10 = k/2^n. Rearranging gives 2^n = 10k, or 2^(n-1) = 5k. The left side has only factors of 2. The right side has a factor of 5. There is no integer k that makes this true. Therefore 0.10 cannot be represented exactly with a finite binary fraction.

That proof is enough to explain why repeated decimal arithmetic can drift. Suppose a system stores the intended unit value x as an approximate value f. The single-row representation error is e = f - x. If a report sums N identical rows and ignores additional rounding during addition, the representation component of the total error is N × e. Real floating-point addition can introduce more rounding at each operation, and aggregate execution order can vary by engine or query plan, but the representation error alone is already sufficient to create a reproducible counterexample.

PostgreSQL’s documentation draws the same high-level distinction for practitioners: numeric supports exact calculations where possible, while real and double precision are inexact, variable-precision numeric types. That does not mean every analytical number must be stored as an exact decimal. It does mean that currency-like repeated decimals should not be treated as harmless just because individual rows look small.

sections.heading: Worked counterexample with a hypothetical retail credit
paragraphs: Use a deliberately small binary representation so the arithmetic fits on the page. This is not a claim about the size of error in a production database or a specific CPU. It is a transparent model that demonstrates the mechanism.

Assume a hypothetical retail events table records a promotional credit of 10 cents for every qualifying event. The intended amount per row is exactly 0.10 dollars, or 1/10. Now assume a toy binary format can store fractions with denominator 8192. The nearest stored value to 0.10 in that toy format is 819/8192, which equals 0.0999755859375.

Now compute the representation error for one row: stored minus intended equals 819/8192 - 1/10. Put those over a common denominator: 8190/81920 - 8192/81920 = -2/81920 = -1/40960. As a decimal, that is -0.0000244140625 dollars per row.

For one row, that is less than one hundredth of a cent. For repeated arithmetic, multiply it. With 100,000 hypothetical events, the exact total is 100,000 × 0.10 = 10,000.00 dollars. The representation-only total in the toy format is 100,000 × 819/8192 = 9,997.55859375 dollars. The error is 100,000 × -1/40960 = -2.44140625 dollars.

This example is intentionally exaggerated by using a tiny toy precision. Binary64 double precision has many more bits, so this example should not be used as a binary64 performance or accuracy estimate. Its value is diagnostic: it proves that a tiny per-row representation difference can become a visible aggregate difference when a decimal amount is repeated enough times.

A useful counterexample falls out of the same arithmetic. If a pipeline stores 0.10 as an approximate binary value and later rounds only the final aggregate to cents, final rounding does not change the fact that the aggregate was computed from the wrong repeated value. In the toy example, rounding the final total to cents gives 9,997.56, not the intended 10,000.00. Presentation rounding can hide small artifacts, but it cannot make approximate input values exact.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style calculation for the toy model.
-- This models the arithmetic with exact numeric values so the counterexample is visible.
WITH hypothetical_events AS (
  SELECT generate_series(1, 100000) AS event_id,
         10::numeric AS intended_cents
), totals AS (
  SELECT
    count(*) AS event_count,
    sum(intended_cents) / 100 AS exact_dollars,
    sum(819::numeric / 8192) AS toy_binary_dollars
  FROM hypothetical_events
)
SELECT
  event_count,
  exact_dollars,
  toy_binary_dollars,
  toy_binary_dollars - exact_dollars AS representation_error
FROM totals;

-- Expected arithmetic:
-- event_count = 100000
-- exact_dollars = 10000.000000...
-- toy_binary_dollars = 9997.55859375
-- representation_error = -2.44140625

sections.heading: Calculation rules for demonstrating the error
paragraphs: When explaining this issue to engineers or analysts, use rules that separate representation from business logic. The goal is not to debate accounting policy, tax treatment, or rounding policy. The goal is to show whether the numeric representation can preserve the intended decimal arithmetic under aggregation.

Rule 1: write the intended decimal as a fraction. For 0.10 dollars, use 1/10. For 0.05, use 1/20. For 0.01, use 1/100. These fractions contain factors of 5 in the denominator, so they are not finite binary fractions unless the factor of 5 cancels away.

Rule 2: write the stored approximation as a fraction. In the toy example, the stored approximation is 819/8192. In a database diagnostic, this may be an actual floating-point value cast or printed with enough precision, but the conceptual rule is the same: compare the stored numeric value to the intended decimal value.
Rule 3: compute per-row error before aggregation. Use e = stored_value - intended_value. This keeps the diagnostic local and makes it clear that even a tiny error has a sign and a magnitude.

Rule 4: multiply by repetition count for a lower-bound demonstration. Use N × e to show the representation component of the aggregate error. If the real execution engine performs floating-point additions in a different order, the final observed residual can differ, but the representation problem has already been established.

Rule 5: compare against an exact control total. The control total should be expressed in minor units, such as cents, or in an exact decimal type. For the hypothetical retail example, the control total is count × 10 cents, not count × an approximate 0.10-dollar float.

These rules also help prevent a common false reassurance: seeing a small number of rows reconcile does not prove that the representation is safe. If an approximate value is slightly high, a small sample may round to the expected cents. If it is slightly low, the same thing can happen. The diagnostic should inspect the residual before presentation rounding and should include realistic repetition counts.
bullets: Represent the intended amount exactly, usually as integer minor units or an exact decimal value.
Represent the approximate value explicitly enough to compute stored minus intended.
Aggregate both paths and compare the residual before display rounding.
Treat the residual as a data quality signal, not as a formatting problem.

sections.heading: A diagnostic query pattern for pipelines
paragraphs: A practical diagnostic compares three totals for the same hypothetical or sampled dataset: an integer-minor-unit control total, an exact decimal total, and the candidate floating-point total. The exact decimal total and integer control should agree for simple currency-like additions. The floating-point total may differ by a tiny amount, by a visible amount, or by an amount that changes with grouping and execution order.

The following query is illustrative PostgreSQL 18 syntax, not evidence of an executed benchmark. It uses generated hypothetical events so the expected control total is obvious. PostgreSQL documents numeric as an exact numeric type and double precision as an inexact type. PostgreSQL’s aggregate documentation also matters because sum is an aggregate operation; once values are aggregated, type choice affects the result you are comparing.

The most useful output column is not the formatted total. It is the residual: candidate_total minus control_total. Run the diagnostic at the grain where the business reconciles numbers: daily revenue, order batch, merchant, product, or settlement file. If many groups are evaluated, summarize the spread of residuals as well as the maximum absolute residual. The NIST handbook’s discussion of measures of scale is a useful general reference for thinking about spread rather than a single example value.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative diagnostic pattern for a hypothetical retail event fixture.
-- The double precision column is included to show the comparison pattern;
-- do not treat any printed floating result here as a cross-platform guarantee.
WITH hypothetical_events AS (
  SELECT
    generate_series(1, 100000) AS event_id,
    10::bigint AS credit_cents
), prepared AS (
  SELECT
    event_id,
    credit_cents,
    credit_cents::numeric / 100 AS credit_numeric_dollars,
    credit_cents::double precision / 100.0::double precision AS credit_float_dollars
  FROM hypothetical_events
), totals AS (
  SELECT
    count(*) AS event_count,
    sum(credit_cents)::numeric / 100 AS control_dollars_from_cents,
    sum(credit_numeric_dollars) AS exact_decimal_dollars,
    sum(credit_float_dollars) AS candidate_float_dollars
  FROM prepared
)
SELECT
  event_count,
  control_dollars_from_cents,
  exact_decimal_dollars,
  candidate_float_dollars,
  exact_decimal_dollars - control_dollars_from_cents AS exact_residual,
  candidate_float_dollars::numeric - control_dollars_from_cents AS float_residual
FROM totals;

sections.heading: What to do with the result
paragraphs: If the diagnostic shows a nonzero floating residual, the conclusion should be precise: the pipeline is using an inexact representation for a repeated decimal amount, and that representation can affect aggregates. That finding does not by itself prescribe tax handling, accounting treatment, materiality thresholds, or how many decimal places a stored value should allow. Those are separate design and policy decisions.

For currency-like analytics, prefer integer minor units when the unit is fixed and known, such as cents for USD-denominated order amounts. This makes addition exact and keeps the control total easy to audit. When values require fractional minor units, variable scales, or non-currency decimal measures, use an exact decimal type with an explicit precision and scale decision. PostgreSQL numeric is designed for exact numeric calculations, but capacity and performance tradeoffs still need to be modeled for the workload.

Avoid using final formatting as the diagnostic. A dashboard that formats a value to two decimal places may hide a small residual until volume grows, grouping changes, or the same metric is reconciled against an exact downstream system. Compare exact and approximate paths before display rounding.

Also avoid treating equality checks on floating aggregates as durable tests. Instead, test the invariant that should be true in exact arithmetic. For the hypothetical coupon credit, the invariant is: total credit cents equals qualifying event count multiplied by 10. That invariant can be evaluated exactly. If the dashboard’s dollar total is computed another way, the residual should be visible in a test or reconciliation query.

The broader modeling lesson is simple: repeated decimal arithmetic deserves an exact path. Floating-point values are useful for many measurements and statistical calculations, but they are a poor default for financial amounts whose correctness is judged by reconciliation against decimal totals.

takeaways: A finite binary floating-point number has a denominator that is a power of two, so common decimals such as 0.10 cannot be represented exactly.
A tiny per-row representation error can become a visible aggregate residual when the same decimal amount is repeated many times.
Demonstrate the issue by comparing an exact control total, usually integer minor units or an exact decimal type, against the candidate floating-point aggregate before presentation rounding.
Keep the conclusion narrow: this is a numeric representation problem, not tax advice, accounting advice, or a complete precision-and-scale design.
